title: Daniel Long: The Reality Behind Building an AI-Powered Law Firm
author: Daniel Long · Philip Young

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source does not address the cluster’s principal claim that automation threatens expertise reproduction or requires reconstructed apprenticeship. It supports only peripheral points about pressure on hourly billing and possible demand expansion, leaving its position on associate training undetermined.
qs: Well, I think one topic that any lawyer listening, I'm sure, is is thinking about is the pricing structure that it doesn't make sense to integrate AI  whilst minimize your time whilst also charging for your time.

it's not deliverable economically whereas AI should change that calculus to make it possible to deliver a lot more work which I think just means that more people will use lawyers for things where historically they hadn't maybe supported by AI products.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Long addresses AI-driven pricing tension, wider service reach and uncertain systemic effects, but does not assess whether automation weakens apprenticeship, expertise development or partner succession routes, nor does he propose funding, simulation, feedback or broader careers as responses.
qs: I think the other interesting question which I haven't got a interesting answer to, but it's what does it mean if legal work suddenly becomes 10 times faster?
But in terms of the actual work that can be done, I guess it, you know, it massively widens where legal services can extend to.

st.t: Neglected claims: AI services target uneconomic legal work
st.an: The source accepts the access-to-justice proposition and materially develops it by explaining how repeatable small-debt processes can be encoded into modular workflows, while linking affordability barriers to a concrete infrastructure proposal for authenticated court APIs and competing private interfaces. Its support remains based on practitioner experience and launch anecdotes rather than systematic evidence of accuracy, recovery rates or scalable economics.
qs: Yeah, I mean I think it's when when we started this and I sketched out on a overly long flowchart the possible  pathways of a small debt claim, it sort of struck me early on that actually a lot of what lawyers do conceptually is very repetitive.
You know, we've got these issues, but like we we couldn't afford the legal work.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that AI delivers bounded gains whose value depends on institutional processes rather than autonomous deployment. It materially extends the synthesis in the small-claims context by showing that court redesign must also account for proportionality, procedural legitimacy and users’ need to feel heard—not merely speed or technical capability.
qs: So I think what you're saying is that AI is helpful but it's not the complete answer because there are other parts of the system that would also have to improve as well.

And if you build a court system that happened in milliseconds I think a lot of people would complain that they don't feel like their case has been heard and listened to even if it was the same outcome.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s claims that AI-generated time savings pressure hourly billing, may prompt fixed or hybrid pricing, and could extend legal services to previously unserved work. It also treats broader systemic effects as unresolved rather than established, while offering little evidence on verification, buyer-side incentives or apprenticeship.
qs: Well, I think one topic that any lawyer listening, I'm sure, is is thinking about is the pricing structure that it doesn't make sense to integrate AI  whilst minimize your time whilst also charging for your time.
There's plenty of our users who would not have hired a lawyer for their work, probably written off much of it.

st.t: Machine judging: Accuracy cannot establish legitimate authority
st.an: The source supports the proposition that accurate or unchanged outcomes would not by themselves legitimate automated adjudication. It emphasises procedural experience and public confidence: people may reject near-instant machine decisions if they do not feel heard or perceive genuine deliberation. It also agrees that AI is only one component of broader court reform, though its claims are predictive rather than empirical.
qs: And if you build a court system that happened in milliseconds I think a lot of people would complain that they don't feel like their case has been heard and listened to even if it was the same outcome.
I think everyone wants to see someone deliberating over their situation and giving it some thought.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central account that AI-driven time savings pressure hourly billing and favour fixed or hybrid pricing, while lower-cost delivery may unlock previously unmet legal demand rather than eliminate lawyers. Its evidence is mainly qualitative and predictive, and it does not materially develop the cluster’s cautions about verification, institutional adoption or autonomous delivery.
qs: Well, I think one topic that any lawyer listening, I'm sure, is is thinking about is the pricing structure that it doesn't make sense to integrate AI  whilst minimize your time whilst also charging for your time.
There's plenty of our users who would not have hired a lawyer for their work, probably written off much of it.

kp.k: Small claims remain difficult despite procedural simplification
kp.d: Long describes delays, unfamiliar terminology and confusing forms in the court system that ordinary users encounter. Young explains that small-claims procedure must remain proportionate to claims involving three or four figures rather than replicate high-value litigation. Drawing on earlier practice and helping his brother-in-law recover unpaid invoices, Young says little had changed over 15–20 years; these are practitioner observations rather than systematic findings.
qs: The small claims court is designed to be easy to use, but in reality there's a lot of unfamiliar terms and forms
not a lot had changed in the sort of 15 20 years between those two periods.

kp.k: Garfield separates deterministic legal logic from AI extraction
kp.d: Long describes a hybrid architecture: an expert system handles procedural timelines, available actions, document compliance and outgoing communications, while AI extracts facts from user material such as invoices. Young adds that the expert system also handles substantive-law issues, including limitation checks during initial triage. Long presents this division as a deliberate response to probabilistic AI's inability to guarantee accuracy, not as evidence of a measured error-free system.
qs: There's an expert system and then there's an AI system and the marrying of those two is really what builds Garfield.
the expert system also does the substantive law parts. A good example being limitation.
if you want 100% accuracy on certain things, AI is unlikely to give 100% accuracy.
we try to make sure that the logic of how the claim should progress is not handled probabilistically.

kp.k: Human document approval precedes automated distribution
kp.d: Long describes Young approving paid-for documents before the expert system distributes them to courts, counterparties and users. The internal review interface gives Young access to conversations and uploaded documents and allows follow-up questions. This is a human-review workflow rather than direct reliance on wholly autonomous output; the transcript supplies no review-time or verification-performance measurements.
qs: when a user is paid for a document and it gets approved by Philip then it's the expert system that will be emailing posting sending it to the court sending to the other party sending it to the user themselves for their records.
The core structure is there where you can see a dialogue, you can see the documents uploaded and then you can contact the user if there's more information needed.

kp.k: More capable models need not replace encoded rules
kp.d: Asked whether future LLMs could reliably assume expert-system work, Long allows the possibility but questions its practical value. Smaller models might reduce latency and cost, but replacing explicit rules could merely save development effort while making production execution less efficient. His position distinguishes technical capability from an economically sensible architecture.
qs: Maybe. I don't know if you'd ever want it to though.
you'd just be saving yourself the hassle of encoding those rules in order to inefficiently run them in production.

kp.k: Conversational interfaces make narrowly scoped legal processes approachable
kp.d: Young reports that users often interact with Garfield like a person or friend rather than an online tool. Long says casual conversation suffices for information gathering, while both describe its persistent focus on small debt claims as intentional. These are founder observations about usability and scope, not comparative user-experience findings.
qs: they they soon start talking to Garfield not as though it's a online tour, but as though it's a person and a friend.
It just needs a casual conversation really.
all it wants to talk about are small debt claims

kp.k: Modular workflows support expansion into additional legal problems
kp.d: Long says the external interaction model could extend to paper-based disputes, with internal review tools expanded for more complicated cases. Standardised stages and actions allow the team to add decision points and document-generation steps. Young argues that conceptual repetition across legal work makes this feasible without equating legal practice with factory work. Expansion remains prospective: Long says they are still refining small debt claims.
qs: externally the user has the model of interaction that can be scaled to any paperbased disputes really.
you can then define all the actions that can be taken at that point within that.
if you step back and think about what you do from a high level, you'll realize that there is a degree of conceptual repetition in most of the tasks.

kp.k: AI efficiency conflicts with billing for time
kp.d: Long argues that reducing time through AI creates tension with hourly charging. He says Garfield began with fixed-cost pricing and suggests traditional law firms might adopt hybrid pricing. The transcript offers a business-model rationale and possible direction of change, not evidence of market-wide pricing adoption.
qs: it doesn't make sense to integrate AI whilst minimize your time whilst also charging for your time.
From our end, it made sense to start with a fixed cost pricing.
if you're a traditional law firm, maybe you have to go for some hybrid pricing

kp.k: Lower delivery costs could unlock unmet legal demand
kp.d: Young predicts that reducing time-intensive legal work, while preserving accuracy and advice quality, should lower delivery costs and ultimately client prices through competition. He expects expanded demand rather than less legal work. As support, he reports a study commissioned by the Law Society and Legal Services Board as finding that 'something like 63%' of people in England and Wales had unmet legal need over a four-year period; he supplies no study title, sample or dates. Long's question about tenfold acceleration is hypothetical, not a measured productivity gain.
qs: should ultimately lead to more competition and therefore be cheaper for clients.
they had found that something like 63% of all people in England and Wales over a 4-year period had had an unmet legal need.
at the moment it's not deliverable economically whereas AI should change that calculus to make it possible to deliver a lot more work
what does it mean if legal work suddenly becomes 10 times faster?

kp.k: Founders report previously uneconomic claims becoming worth pursuing
kp.d: Long reports launch feedback from friends unable to afford legal work or spare the time, and says many users would otherwise have written claims off. He also relays clients' reports of faster, less troublesome recovery. Young says some users reported deploying recovered money to expand businesses and hire employees. These are anecdotes carried by the provider, with no customer counts, recovery totals or independently measured employment effects.
qs: There's plenty of our users who would not have hired a lawyer for their work, probably written off much of it.
it was so much faster, so much less hassle. We probably were just going to write these things off.
they've been able to expand, take on new employees and things like that.

kp.k: Authorisation delayed launch and exposed commercial uncertainty
kp.d: Long says reaching regulated and authorised status took considerable time, during which he worried that the product might attract no users. This is an account of the provider's route to launch, not an explanation of a particular regulatory regime or professional rule; neither the regulator nor specific authorisation requirements are identified in this discussion.
qs: it took us a long time to get to the point where we were regulated and authorized.
I was worrying that we were going to launch and then no one's going to be interested, no one was going to use it.

kp.k: Model selection should reflect task requirements and costs
kp.d: Long argues that many applications already have sufficient LLM capability for substantial economic impact and need not use the newest foundation models. He reports Gemini 3's performance on abstract-reasoning benchmarks, naming the 'ARK 2 challenge', as a reason to question plateau narratives, but provides no scores or evaluation details. Young agrees with task-specific selection. These are assessments of the model ecosystem, not measured legal-task results.
qs: you don't need the latest foundation model for a lot of tasks
Gemini 3 comes out and it smashes the benchmarks and it also importantly smashes benchmarks that like the ARK 2 challenge which specifically tests more abstract reasoning
already there's huge number of applications where LLMs are at a point where they can already have huge a huge economic impact

kp.k: Public model availability raises competing access and safety concerns
kp.d: Young favours good publicly available models and worries about increasing proprietary control, while acknowledging uncertainty about his claim that Meta had stopped public releases. He predicts public models will lag frontier offerings for economic reasons. Long introduces AI 2027 as a counterpoint, and both acknowledge that open-source or open-weight availability may facilitate misuse. These are views and speculative trade-offs, not established findings about model availability or safety.
qs: there's also an increasing degree of proprietary control over LLM.
it would be better for society if there are good publicly available LLB models.
Some some people who are not well-intentioned may then use those technologies for very unwise things.

kp.k: Institutional constraints limit end-to-end AI productivity gains
kp.d: Long rejects expectations of instantaneous transformation: providers operate within existing court processes, so agentic capability alone cannot accelerate the entire system. He expects successive, bounded improvements rather than a single enormous productivity spike. Young elaborates that court modernisation requires development, testing and deployment, creating time lags even where AI improves provider productivity.
qs: we can apply AI but we're constrained by the system that we work within.
you can't just let an agent loose on the small claims court and expect instantaneous change.
you're going to see this sort of steady increase rather than this like giant exponential climb.
AI is helpful but it's not the complete answer because there are other parts of the system that would also have to improve as well.

kp.k: Perceived deliberation may constrain acceptance of instantaneous justice
kp.d: Long speculates that even outcome-equivalent adjudication in milliseconds could leave users feeling unheard. He compares this with patients needing time to trust near-instant machine interpretation of medical scans. The argument concerns perceived procedural legitimacy and acceptance, not evidence that slower decisions are more accurate or a measured public preference.
qs: if you build a court system that happened in milliseconds I think a lot of people would complain that they don't feel like their case has been heard and listened to even if it was the same outcome.
I think everyone wants to see someone deliberating over their situation and giving it some thought.

kp.k: Courts should provide APIs while providers compete on interfaces
kp.d: Long recommends that government, the civil service and courts build simple RESTful APIs accessible to authenticated systems, leaving private providers to compete over user-facing interfaces. He expects competitive feedback to improve usability and drive interface margins towards zero, contrasting this with weaker competitive incentives in public-sector interface development. Young endorses using competition in this way; this is a policy proposal, not a description of existing infrastructure or demonstrated price effects.
qs: build really simple restful APIs that systems can integrate with
obviously they have to be authenticated systems in order to make those requests
leave the private sector to compete and reduce the margins down to basically zero over the front ends, the UIs for those systems
in the private sector there's a strong incentive to build a system that users really like using

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Daniel Long describes reliable small-debt-claim automation as a combination of deterministic legal workflows, AI information extraction and human document approval—not an LLM autonomously managing litigation.
pts.d: Long says Garfield's expert system manages procedural timings, available actions, compliant document generation and outgoing communications, while AI extracts facts from users and documents. Philip Young adds that the expert system also handles substantive-law checks such as limitation. Long describes documents being approved by Young before the expert system distributes them. These are founders' accounts of the existing product, not independently measured accuracy findings; the statement that processes need to work with 100% reliability is a requirement, not a reported result.

pts.k: Long doubts that improved LLMs will make replacing explicitly encoded legal rules desirable, even if doing so becomes technically feasible.
pts.d: Asked whether LLMs could reliably take over work now performed by the expert system, Long gives a qualified rather than categorical answer. Smaller models with lower latency and cost might permit more logic to move into models, but he sees little benefit in exchanging the work of encoding rules for less efficient production execution. This is a forward-looking technical judgment grounded in his development experience, with no adoption date or comparative performance measurements.

pts.k: Long says conversational interaction can make a tightly scoped legal process easier to navigate by eliciting the information needed without requiring formal legal prose.
pts.d: Long reports that most users interact conversationally with Garfield and that the system can also handle letter-style submissions. He acknowledges its narrow focus on small debt claims: the claimed benefit is guided interaction within a constrained service, not general legal competence. The evidence is internal observation of user conversations, without usability-study results or quantified completion rates.

pts.k: Long predicts that Garfield's modular architecture can extend beyond small debt claims to other paper-based disputes and high-volume, low-risk legal applications.
pts.d: Long identifies reusable external interaction design, internal document-review tooling and modular decision stages as the basis for expansion. More complicated cases would require changes to the review interface, and the team is still refining the small-debt-claim service. The prediction rests on the architecture the founders have built, not evidence that the additional legal services have already been deployed. No expansion timetable is given.

pts.k: Long argues that AI time savings create tension with hourly billing and encourage fixed-price or hybrid pricing models.
pts.d: Long presents this as a current business-model issue for traditional firms, contrasting their potential transition with Garfield's decision to begin with fixed-cost pricing. Hybrid pricing is a possibility, not a definite prediction of universal replacement of the billable hour. No fee comparisons, profitability data or survey of law firms is supplied.

pts.k: Long claims that AI-enabled services expand the reachable legal market by making it practical to pursue matters that users would otherwise abandon.
pts.d: Long cites Garfield users who would not have hired a lawyer and would probably have written off their claims, along with messages from acquaintances describing unaffordable legal work and insufficient time. He reports customer feedback that the service is faster and less troublesome. This is qualitative evidence of unmet need and customer experience, rather than a measured estimate of the service's market-wide effect. His question about legal work or disputes becoming ten times faster is a hypothetical, not an achieved speed-up.

pts.k: Philip Young, presenting his own view as co-founder, predicts that lower production costs and competition will make legal help cheaper and unlock additional demand rather than simply reduce legal work.
pts.d: Young's mechanism is that reducing time spent on document-heavy tasks lowers delivery costs, which should ultimately produce more competition and lower client prices. He explicitly conditions this on maintaining accuracy and advice quality. As evidence of latent demand, he recalls a study commissioned by the Law Society and Legal Services Board as finding that roughly 63% of people in England and Wales had an unmet legal need over four years. The transcript supplies neither the study title nor survey dates or methodology; the statistic is preserved as Young's characterization, not an independently established finding. He distinguishes the cited consumer market from additional business-market opportunities.

pts.k: Long argues that many economically useful AI applications already do not require the latest foundation model, while expecting continued frontier-model progress.
pts.d: Long anticipates, and says there is already some, differentiation in model choice according to tasks and running costs. He cites the newly released Gemini 3 and what the transcript calls the 'ARK 2 challenge' as evidence that abstract-reasoning performance is improving. He supplies no benchmark scores or legal-task validation; the benchmark discussion supports his general model-capability outlook, not a demonstrated rate of improvement in legal services. His claim that no limits appear to be reached is explicitly based on what he reads.

pts.k: Long predicts that institutional constraints will make AI-driven improvement gradual rather than an instantaneous transformation of dispute resolution.
pts.d: Long distinguishes technical capability from the pace of change possible within the court system, describing successive S-shaped improvements rather than an unlimited exponential rise. He also suggests that perceived fairness and trust constrain how quickly people will accept near-instant adjudication: litigants may want visible deliberation even if outcomes are unchanged. These are qualitative predictions and experience-based judgments, not measured productivity or public-attitude findings.

pts.k: Long proposes public court APIs combined with competing private interfaces, predicting that this division would improve usability and drive down interface-provider margins.
pts.d: Long recommends that government, the civil service and courts provide simple RESTful APIs for authenticated systems, leaving private providers to compete over user-facing services. His causal claim is that private competition creates stronger incentives for simple, useful interfaces than public-sector interface development does. Near-zero margins are an envisaged competitive outcome, not a current observation or quantified forecast. Implementation depends on courts making interoperable infrastructure available.

pts.k: Young claims that recovering otherwise lost debts through Garfield has helped some business clients expand and hire employees.
pts.d: This is Young's own report of customer feedback, offered as a counterexample to accounts focused solely on AI job losses. It concerns employment in client businesses, not evidence of increased law-firm employment or a net positive employment effect across the economy. No customer counts, recovered sums or job totals are provided.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The legal-service claims are supported mainly by founders' implementation experience and anecdotal user feedback; broader forecasts rely on causal reasoning and limited references to external evidence.
pts.d: Long draws on approximately two and a half years building Garfield, observing conversations and hearing post-launch feedback. Young contributes practice experience, users' reported business outcomes and an incompletely identified unmet-need study. Long's model-progress claims invoke general benchmarks without scores. The transcript provides no independent evaluation of Garfield, quantified error rates, controlled time-saving comparison, price series or market-wide employment analysis. Architectural descriptions, observed customer experiences, hypothetical scenarios and predictions should therefore remain distinct.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Current product descriptions and post-launch observations are distinct from undated expansion and market forecasts, which depend on accuracy, suitable tasks and institutional adaptation.
pts.d: The source is labelled 2026 and describes roughly two and a half years of development. Existing capabilities concern small debt claims and a workflow involving human document approval. Additional modules, model substitution, pricing evolution and demand expansion have no firm deadlines. Long conditions wider application on success in the initial service and acknowledges remaining refinements. He stresses court-system constraints and user acceptance. The four-year window in Young's cited statistic describes unmet-need experience, not a forecast period; its calendar dates are unspecified. The tenfold acceleration example is hypothetical.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The central beneficiaries are people and businesses with economically neglected small claims; the predicted changes also affect law-firm pricing, legal-service providers and court infrastructure.
pts.d: Individuals and businesses unable to justify conventional legal costs are described as gaining a practical route to debt recovery and legal assistance. Some business clients reportedly reinvest recoveries in growth and hiring. Traditional firms face tension between time-saving technology and hourly revenue, while lawyers may gain demand from previously unserved matters. Reviewing lawyers remain involved in the described product workflow. Developers and competing service providers would benefit from court APIs, with competitive pressure on interface margins. Courts and policymakers face infrastructure and legitimacy constraints, and litigants may value being visibly heard as well as receiving a rapid outcome. The source does not make a concrete prediction about associate staffing structures or lawyer headcount.
